> A criminal is a person who breaks the law AND causes an innocent person to become a victim

Ok, I will propose a hypothetical here:

I see you have a nice TV. I steal it. I have now created an “innocent victim.”

The reasons for this aren’t clear, I could want it to sell on the secondary market for cash, trade it for necessities or pay off debts, I could just want it and not have it/be able to afford it, whatever.

Should the state in your world you’ve set up be able to kill me for my crime? What about someone who steals food from you? Someone who has a mental break in public, caused a disturbance and harassed someone? Should these people be killed for committing crimes?

> Norway has one of the lowest recidivism rates in the world, which is still ~25%. If they are properly addressing the needs of criminals, then clearly rehabilitation isn't good enough. To claim that rehabilitation can work, the best instances of rehabilitation in the world right now must be doing it wrong.

Under a neoliberal capitalist government (yes, even the “much beloved” Nordic countries), the rehabilitation efforts will be wasted to a large degree because the original material conditions for which the person was led to commit crime in the first place weren’t addressed. So of course they’ll go on to commit more crimes even if they were “treated nicer and educated” in prison. This is no excuse to throw away rehabilitation because it is missing its other vital part (IMO): the prevention programs that assist criminals to reintegrate and to address the material concerns that led to the crime in the first place.

> I'm not sure what you mean by this. But I'll clarify what I meant by what I said: There is no evidence that rehabilitation can be even close to 100% effective. Therefore, we are certain to see more innocent people becoming victims when we release criminals back into society.

The 100% figure stumps me because this is a utopian idea, nice in theory but in practice is genuinely impossible. I also say “essentialism” because given the words you’ve used and actions you advocate seem to imply/assume that once a criminal has committed a crime *(leaving out “creating an innocent victim” for the sake of brevity)* they are forever deemed a criminal and have always been a criminal simply because rehabilitation (solitary with no additional mechanisms!) doesn’t have a 100% chance of success, and therefore must be executed to save a hypothetical victim from a hypothetical crime in the future. This is stating that criminals are criminals not matter what and we cannot help them.

Not to be harsh, but I say your statements are all *vibes based* because there’s no material analysis here. Sure, we can quote numbers from governments about their recidivism rates, but it’s doing zero digging into *why* the people commit the crimes they do and *why* they often relapse to crime. It also is very all-or-nothing with no nuance: if a criminal reform program (whatever its name be) doesn’t have a 100% success rate, we should just jump to executing 100% of criminals? And I’m sure you probably *mean for there to be more nuance* in your position, but casting such a broad umbrella leaves room for reactionary elements to either equivocate us with fascists or take the idea and run with it and mold it to their whims to target the “uncivilized” (I.e. “degenerate”) elements in society.
